paragraphs.text: Kayla groaned as she joined Kobe and Jenny at a table. "I hate science experiments."
"Science experiments are fun," Jenny said. "We just need a good idea."
Kayla sighed. "I'm sick of making volcanoes explode."
"We could grow mold," Kobe said.
Jenny made a face. "Mold is gross."
Kayla looked bored. She ripped a sheet of paper from her notebook.
Jenny frowned. "Mr. Netter said we're supposed to work together, Kayla. You're not helping us."
Kayla was folding wings on a paper airplane. "Let's test this plane."
"Huh?" Kobe said.
"We can measure how far it flies," Kayla said.
"Good idea!" Kobe said.
"It sounds scientific and fun," Jenny agreed. She looked at her notebook. "Step one of the scientific method is to ask questions."
"How about, how does weight affect flight distance?" Kobe said.
Everyone nodded.
Jenny wrote down the question. "Next we have to come up with a hypothesis. That's a guess about what will happen."
The kids did some research about airplane flight.
"Hmm," said Kayla. "I think a lighter plane will fly farther."
"Me too," Kobe said. "That's our hypothesis: a light paper plane will fly farther."
Jenny wrote it down. "To test our hypothesis, we'll have to change the plane's weight."
Kobe got some paperclips. "We can use these to add weight."
Kayla grabbed her airplane. "Let's find a runway!"
The kids went out into the hallway. Kayla threw the plane and Kobe measured where it stopped.
"My turn!" said Kobe.
"We should try to throw the plane the same way each time," said Jenny. "So Kayla should keep flying the plane."
Kayla flew the plane several more times and Kobe measured each flight's distance.
Next they added two paperclips to the plane. They flew and measured several more times.
Jenny recorded the results.
"Let's try four paperclips now," Kayla said.
They flew the plane again.
"Time to analyze our data!" Kobe said.
"Uh-oh." Jenny studied the results with a frown. "Our plane flew farthest with two paperclips. Our hypothesis was incorrect."
"That's okay," Kobe said. "Mr. Netter said a science experiment is for testing ideas. Even if your hypothesis is incorrect, you still learn stuff."
Kayla grinned. "I learned something—science experiments can be fun!"
Megan was brushing her teeth.
She left the water running.
Sam banged on the door.
"It's Earth Day!" he said. "Don't waste water!"
Downstairs Dad collected bottles.
Mom collected paper.
"Recycling is good for the earth," said Dad.
After breakfast Megan gathered food scraps.
She and Dad took them outside to the compost.
"Compost is good for the garden," said Dad.
Megan saw a strange box in the yard.
"What's that box?" asked Megan.
"You'll see later," said Dad with a wink.
Mom and Sam came outside.
"Let's go grocery shopping," said Mom.
"Okay," Megan said.
"I'll get lunch ready here," said Dad.
Megan stepped toward the car.
"Let's walk," said Mom.
"It's better for the environment."
At the store a clerk got some plastic bags.
"No thanks. We brought canvas shopping bags," said Mom.
"They are better for the earth."
Everyone was hungry after the long walk home.
"I smell pizza!" said Megan.
"Remember the box?" said Dad.
"It's a solar oven!"
"Awesome! The sun cooked the pizza," said Megan.
"I love Earth Day!"
It was Christmas Eve. Speedy and Boomer were about to start their new job.
The two reindeer looked around the warehouse. They saw a huge, pretty sleigh. Colorful presents filled tall shelves. Elves scurried around everywhere.
"Hey there!" said a friendly voice.
Speedy and Boomer turned around.
"I'm Rudolph," said a reindeer with a shiny red nose. "I'm the reindeer in charge. Our job tonight is to pull that sleigh through the air."
"That sounds easy," said Boomer.
Rudolph nodded. "It's not hard. But our boss, Santa, has lots of stops to make. We'll stop at millions of houses all over the world."
"Whoa!" Speedy gasped. "One night isn't enough time!"
"Don't worry," said Rudolph. "We will have 24 hours of night."
"Huh?" said Boomer. "How is that possible?"
Rudolph led Boomer and Speedy to a giant map.
"Earth is divided into 24 time zones," said Rudolph.
"Because there are 24 hours in one day?" asked Speedy.
"Right," said Rudolph. "The sun only shines on one side of Earth at a time. So it's always daytime in some places and nighttime in others."
"Let me show you." Rudolph pressed a button. A big part of the map went dark.
"When it's 11:00 p.m. in Japan, it's only 11:00 a.m. in Argentina," Rudolph said. "Argentina's time is 12 hours behind Japan's."
He pressed another button. A zigzag line appeared.
"This is the International Date Line," said Rudolph. "Each day starts here. We'll start at this line and fly west."
"How long will we spend in each time zone?" asked Speedy.
"One hour. Then we'll move west to the next time zone," said Rudolph.
"Oh! The time will be one hour earlier there!" said Boomer.
"Exactly!" said Rudolph. "We should get ready. We have 24 time zones to visit!"
"That's a lot of flying," said Boomer. "I'm going to get hungry."
"Many children leave treats for us," said Rudolph. "But watch out—the boss usually eats them all!"
Hi! My name is Dan. Do you see that fire down there? I'm going to jump down to it with my parachute! No, I'm not doing it for fun. I'm a special kind of firefighter called a smoke jumper.

Smoke jumpers are trained to fight fires in the wilderness. During training we learn how to use parachutes. We also learn different ways to fight fire. Finally we focus on becoming stronger and fitter. This helps us prepare for the dangerous work ahead.

When smoke jumpers get called to fight fire, we must act fast. Airplanes carry us over the fire. Then we jump down with our parachutes. Planes drop our supplies, which include water, food, and fire-fighting tools. We usually have everything we need for about three days.

Once we're on the ground, it's time to start fighting the fire. Sometimes we spray water at the flames. Helicopters also dump it from the air. But wildfires can be massive! So we often have to try something else. We build a fire line.
A fire line is a barrier that blocks fire. You see, wildfires need fuel like dry trees and plants to keep burning. So our goal is to destroy the fuel!
We start building the fire line by cutting down trees with chainsaws. We clear plants away. We even use fire to stop wildfire. We burn smaller things like wood chips to clear the land.
The wildfire keeps spreading until it reaches our fire line. Once it arrives, we hope our work pays off! Without fuel, the wildfire should slow down or even die out.

Not all wildfires are bad. Some even help forests survive! Over time forests can get too crowded with plants and trees. Wildfires clear out the area. They also improve the soil. New plants can grow healthy and strong.

Lightning causes some wildfires. But sadly people cause more of them. Sometimes campers forget to watch their campfires. Or they don't completely put them out before leaving the forest. The fire starts back up, and soon it's burning out of control.
Earth's weather is changing a lot. Many places don't get enough rain, drying out forests and grasslands. Because of this, wildfires are a growing problem.
Luckily smoke jumpers are trained to help. It's a dangerous job, but I love it! I travel all over, fighting wildfires.
It's time for me to jump. So long!
Hello! I'm Kat, and I'm a helicopter pilot. Today I have an important mission. A man was hiking in the mountains and got hurt. I'm transporting rescue workers to the mountain to help him.
Helicopters are great rescue vehicles. Climb aboard mine, and I'll tell you why.

See that airplane? It needs a long airstrip to take off and land. Helicopters don't need that. They can lift straight up off the ground! And they can land in places where an airplane can't land. That makes them perfect for rescue missions like this one.
While we fly, I'll explain how helicopters work.
My helicopter has two rotors. The main rotor sits on top of the helicopter. It spins really fast. I can control it with this lever.
Two long wings are attached to the rotor. They're called rotor blades. When the rotor spins, the blades spin too. They push air down. That makes the helicopter go up.
I can also control the tilt of the rotor blades. By doing that, I can make the helicopter go in different directions.

My helicopter's second rotor is attached to the helicopter's tail. It's smaller than the main one but just as important. Here's why. The main rotor blades spin in one direction. That makes the helicopter spin in the opposite direction. Nobody wants that to happen. We'd all get dizzy! So the tail rotor blades must spin too. That keeps the helicopter steady, stopping it from spinning out of control.
Helicopters can't go as fast or as high as airplanes. But they can go up and down, sideways and backward. They can also move slowly over the land. This will help us spot the hurt hiker.
Oh! There he is!

Hmm. He's on a trail with a steep slope. I don't see anywhere safe for me to land my helicopter. But that's okay. I know what to do. Unlike planes, helicopters can stay up in the air, in one spot. I'll keep my helicopter right here. A rescue worker can go down to help the hiker.
Good news! The rescue worker is back in the helicopter with the hiker. Everyone is safe. Off we go to the hospital.
We're almost there. Do you see that big circle with an H on the roof? I can gently land my helicopter on it.
Well, my work is done. I'm heading back to the airport!
It is March.
It is almost spring.
Today I will grow an herb.
The herb is rosemary.
I push seeds in the dirt and cover them.
I whisper to my tray every day.
"Grow, Little Rosemary, grow!" I say.
I run to Little Rosemary every day.
I water Little Rosemary every day.
She grows inside the dirt.
I wait and wait.
Then I see something green.
I put her by the window.
The sun shines.
Little Rosemary grows more leaves.
Little Rosemary smells good.
Little Rosemary is tall.
I plant her in the garden.
I am glad Little Rosemary is here.
I grew her by myself.
Seeds don't have feet or wings.
But some seeds can travel.
This is a dandelion seed.
How does this seed travel?
The wind helps this seed travel.
"Whee! Farther! Farther!"
This is a willow tree seed.
How does this seed travel?
The river helps this seed travel.
"Watch me float!"
This is a cherry seed.
How does this seed travel?
The bird helps this seed travel.
The bird's poop carries the seed to the ground.
This is a sunflower seed.
How does this seed travel?
The rain helps this seed fall to the ground.
"Look out! Get out of my way!"
This is an impatiens seed.
How does this seed travel?
This seed pops onto the ground.
"I am an acrobat!"
This is a Spanish needles seed.
How does this seed travel?
People help this seed travel.
This seed sticks to the girl's sweater. "Ouch!"
Some seeds are really good travelers.
"Thank you for the ride!"
A lot of Samantha's friends wore glasses. Henry's glasses made him look smart. Glasses made shy Emma stand out. Jenna had several pairs of glasses. She liked her glasses to match her clothes!
Samantha wanted to look smarter and more stylish too.
"Mom," said Samantha. "I need glasses."
"Do you have trouble seeing at school?" asked Mom.
"Um," said Samantha quickly. "Sometimes."
"I'll make an appointment to see the optometrist," said Mom.
Samantha and Mom went to Dr. Green's office the next day. Samantha felt bad. She thought she could see fine. She just wanted glasses!
Dr. Green asked Samantha to read a chart with rows of letters. It wasn't easy! The letters at the bottom looked small and blurry. She couldn't read them.
Dr. Green sat down to talk to Samantha and Mom.
"You're nearsighted, Samantha," said Dr. Green.
"What does that mean?" asked Samantha. She wanted glasses, but she didn't want problems with her vision!
"Nearsighted people see things close up normally," said Dr. Green. "But faraway things look blurry."
Dr. Green showed them a model of a round eyeball. "The eyeball in nearsighted people is a little too long," he explained. "In farsighted people the eyeball is too short."
"Is this because Samantha reads so much?" asked Mom.
"Too much reading doesn't cause the problem. But it's good to take breaks to avoid eye strain or headaches," said Dr. Green.
"Being nearsighted can be caused by family history or the environment," Dr. Green continued.
"I heard eating carrots helps you see," said Samantha.
"Carrots and oily fish like salmon have vitamin A," said Dr. Green. "So do dark leafy vegetables. Vitamin A helps keep eyes healthy."
"Will it fix my eyes?" asked Samantha.

"It won't cure your eyes." Dr. Green smiled. "Spend more time outdoors in the sunshine. Scientists believe that it slows children's eyes from becoming nearsighted. For now, glasses will help you see clearly."
Samantha chose her new glasses.
"I look great!" she said. "And I can see better!"
"Let me see how you look," said Mom. She squinted and then leaned closer to Samantha.
"Wow! You do look good," said Mom. "But maybe I need to make an appointment for myself!"
"Class, we're going to get a class pet," said Mrs. Frink. "We need to decide what kind of pet."
Eric raised his hand. "I want a dog!"
"No way!" said Pearl. "Dogs chew everything!"
"A dog is not a good class pet," said Mrs. Frink. "Dogs need too much care."
"I like hamsters," said Alice.
"Let's get a giraffe!" said Owen.
Everybody laughed.
Mrs. Frink frowned. "Please be serious, Owen."
More kids shouted ideas. The classroom was very noisy.
Mrs. Frink held up a hand. "Let's take a poll," she said. "We'll each vote for the pet we want."
The teacher passed out pieces of paper for voting. When everyone was done, Mrs. Frink collected the papers.
"Now we'll count the votes," she said. "We'll make a bar graph. Then we’ll see which pet got the most votes."
Mrs. Frink drew a graph on the whiteboard.
"Let's write numbers along the left side of the graph," said Mrs. Frink. "And let’s write pets at the bottom of the graph."
Mrs. Frink read the first vote. "One vote for hamster."
Alice wrote "hamster" at the bottom of the graph. She colored up to the 1.
Then Mrs. Frink read another vote. Alice added that to the graph. Soon the bar graph was almost full.
"Boo!" said Alice. "Hamster got just one vote!"
"Giraffe got two votes!" Owen laughed.
"I see four votes for fish," said Pearl. "That's what I voted for!"
"Hedgehog got four votes too," said Eric. "It’s a tie!"
"No, there’s one more vote," said Mrs. Frink. She colored one of the bars on the graph. "So, what pet will we get?"
"A hedgehog!" The class cheered.
Theo walked into the kitchen. His mom was cooking.
"What's for dinner?" he asked.
"I'm making your favorite food," said Mom. "Macaroni and cheese."
"Yum!" said Theo. Then he saw some spinach and carrots.
"Yuck!" said Theo. "What are those vegetables for?"
"They're for a salad," said Mom. "It has salmon and vegetables."
"Salmon!" cried Theo. "No, thanks. I'm just going to eat macaroni and cheese."
"You can't eat just that," said Mom. "You need food from all five food groups."
"Macaroni and cheese has stuff from two food groups," said Theo. "The macaroni is a grain, and the cheese is a dairy food. Isn't that enough?"
"You need vegetables too. Carrots have vitamin A," said Mom. She started chopping some carrots. "Vitamin A is good for your eyes."
"Is salmon good for us?" asked Theo.
"Salmon is in the protein group," said Mom. "Protein helps build muscles."
"Okay," said Theo. "So far dinner includes grains, vegetables, dairy, and protein. But you said there are five food groups."
Just then Dad came in from the garden. He had a basket of strawberries.
"The other group is fruits," Mom said. "We're having strawberries for dessert."
"Yum!" said Theo.
Mom grinned. "See? Healthy foods are delicious!"
"I'm still not sure about that salad," Theo said. "But I will try it!"
"Dad," Ricky said one day. "When I grow up, I want to be an Arctic explorer."
"Really?" said Dad. "Why?"
"The Arctic is so cool!" said Ricky. "We learned about it in class. I want to see polar bears and Arctic foxes."
"That's great," said Dad. "But can you live there?"
Ricky thought about it for a while. "Is living in the Arctic very hard?" he asked.
"Yes," said Dad. "Did you know it's always light during summer?"
"No," said Ricky. "But that would be awesome!"
"And it's always dark during winter," said Dad.
"Oh," said Ricky. "That's not so awesome."
"It gets very cold in the Arctic," Dad continued. "Hot water can turn to ice right away!"
Ricky hugged himself and shivered.
"So you see, son," said Dad. "It is not easy to live in the Arctic."
"I think I can do it," said Ricky. "But I need to start training right away. And I'll need your help."
"All right. What can I do?" asked Dad.
"Can you add five dollars to my weekly allowance?" asked Ricky.
"How will that help?" asked Dad.
"Well," said Ricky. "I can buy ice cream with the money. That will help me get used to the cold!"
I planted red bell pepper seeds today.
First, I put the seeds in a pot.
Next, I covered them with soil.
Then, I watered them.
This morning I checked the pepper pot.
I didn't see anything.
Are roots growing in the soil?
Today I saw a green sprout!
A tiny stem is poking through the soil.
Yay!
The stem gets taller each day.
Leaves are growing.
My pepper seedling looks strong.
This morning I planted the seedling in the backyard.
The sunny backyard is good for the plant.
Today I looked at my pepper plant.
I saw many small buds on it.
Flowers will grow from those buds.
Now flowers are blooming on the plant!
The tiny white flowers are so pretty.
Hmm. The flowers died quickly.
But the plant has tiny green peppers!
The peppers are changing color.
Some are still green.
But some are turning red!
All my peppers are red now.
That means they're finally ripe.
I pick one and take a bite.
Yum!
"Good morning, class" said Mr. Aron. "Today we have a visitor."
Jada looked up. The visitor was Miss Santiago, the school nurse.
"Is somebody sick?" asked Paul.
The nurse smiled and shook her head. "I'm here to talk about food allergies."
"Ooh!" Mike waved his arm. "I'm allergic to peanuts!"
"I'm allergic to shrimp," said Matt.
"I can't eat eggs," said Jennifer.
"My sister is allergic to tree nuts," said Jada.
"What happens if you eat these things?" asked Miss Santiago.
"I get a bad stomachache," said Matt. "Then I throw up!"
"I get itchy," said Jennifer.
"Are food allegies dangerous?" asked Carly.
"They can be dangerous," said the nurse. "Some kids have severe allergies. Foods can stop their breathing. But there's medicine to help."
Jennifer raised her hand. "If you're allergic to foods, what can you do?"
"Good question, Jennifer," said Miss Santiago. "Anyone have an idea? How can you protect yourself?"
"Always check food labels," said Carly.
"Don't trade food with other kids," said Mike.
"Carry your allergy medicine everywhere!" said Jada.
"Great ideas!" said Miss Santiago. "You must also speak up. Tell teachers and friends. Make sure everyone knows about your allergy. That will keep you healthy."
Paul raised his hand. "I have a severe allergy. But it's not a food allergy."
"What is it then, Paul?" asked Mr. Aron.
Paul grinned. "Ah-choo! I'm allergic to homework!"
Spring is beginning.
I open the window.
The air is fresh.
The animals are waking up.
I watch the animals.
They stretch and yawn.
The flowers are blooming.
I smell the flowers.
They smell good.
The grass is growing.
I look at the grass.
It is so green.
The birds are singing.
I listen to the birds.
They are in their nest.
My friends are waving.
I wave too.
I think about picnics.
My friends are sitting.
I lie down.
We feel the cool breeze.
It is raining!
We get wet!
We say good-bye and run home!
Mercury, number one.
It is the closest to the sun.
Venus bright, number two.
Morning and evening star we view.
Planet Earth, number three.
We live on it, you and me.
Planet Mars, number four.
Named after the Roman god of war.
Number five, Jupiter.
Colored clouds around it stir.
Number six, big Saturn.
Many rings around it turn.
Number seven, Uranus.
It looks blue and green to us.
Number eight, stormy Neptune.
Triton is its frozen moon.
The eight planets that we know.
Round and round the sun they go.

I like spring because it's warm.
I have new flowers and leaves.
The bees visit me.
Ahhh! Spring.
I like summer because it's hot.
My apples are big. My leaves are green.
People have picnics.
Hmmm! Summer.
I like autumn because it's cool.
My apples are red. My leaves are colorful.
People pick apples.
Wow! Autumn.
I like winter because it's cold.
My apples fall off. My leaves fall off.
People make snowmen.
Brrr! Winter.
It's a dark day.
The sky is gray.
And the air is cool.
Not much to do.
It's the end of winter.
It's a gloomy day.
The snow is melting away.
The trees have no leaves.
Not much to see.
It's the end of winter.
It's a slow day.
The butterflies are away.
The animals are inside.
Nature is hiding.
It's the end of winter.
It's a boring day.
There are no kids outside at play.
My bike and ball are packed.
My tent and rope are stacked.
It's the end of winter.
But soon!
It will be a bright day.
The sun will shine its rays.
And the air will warm our hearts.
There'll be lots of games to start.
It will be spring.
It will be a happy day.
The grass will be green and straight.
The trees will get fresh new blooms.
There'll be lots to do.
It will be spring.
It will be a busy day.
The butterflies will dance and sway.
The animals will be running.
Nature will be stunning.
It will be spring.
It will be a fun day.
I will ride my bike a long way.
I will jump rope with my friends.
We will play outside until the day ends.
It will be spring.
I will be very happy.
It makes me want to sing.
But for now,
I can only dream of spring.

The air is getting colder.
Jack and Sally go out to play.
"Look at the squirrel! What is he doing?"
"I'm not sure."
"What are you doing, Mr. Squirrel?"
"I'm gathering nuts."
"Can we help?"
"Oh yes, please."
"What are the birds doing?"
"I'll ask. Mr. Bird, what are you doing?"
"We're flying away for the winter."
"Can we come?"
"No, you cannot. I don't think you can fly."
"What is your uncle doing, Jack?"
"I don't know."
"Uncle Steve, what are you doing?"
"I'm picking apples."
"Can we help?"
"Sure you can."
"Hey, what is your mother doing? That looks like fun!"
"Not sure.
"Mom, what are you doing?"
"I'm carving a pumpkin."
"Can we help?"
"Of course, there are many pumpkins to carve."
"Look at your dad! What is your dad doing?"
"I don't know."
"Dad, what are you doing?"
"I'm raking leaves."
"Can we help?"
"Okay, I guess you can. Here are the rakes."
"What a big pile of leaves!"
"Do you want to jump into them?"
"Yeah, let's jump." "Wee! Wee!"
"Oh no! What a mess!"
Hello! My name is Drizzle.
I am a tiny water drop.
Whew! The sun is heating me up!
I am getting smaller and smaller.
Oh! I am going up, up, up into a cloud! Whee!
Look at them.
They look just like me.
It is really cool up here.
I like this place.
Hey! Look at me!
I am getting bigger and bigger.
Oh no! I am too big and heavy!
I am falling from the sky!
Where am I now?
Oh! I am in a river.
My friends are falling onto the ground.
They are seeping into the ground.
Now this river is moving fast!
Oh no! A waterfall!
What is this place?
Oh! I am being cleaned!
It's dark in here.
Where am I going now?
Ohh! "Splash!"
Wow! Here I am again!

We all need water to wash our hands and faces.
Water is wonderful!
Mommy needs water to make lemonade.
Water is wonderful!
Farmers need water to grow fruits and vegetables.
Water is wonderful!
Dams need water to make electricity.
Water is wonderful!
Firefighters need water to put out fires.

Water is wonderful!
